DC Versus AC, Transformers, and Wall Power

Unit 3: Electricity and Electronics. Lesson 15 of 53 in BMET Academy.

There are two kinds of electricity in every hospital room, and the boundary between them sits inside each device's power supply. Knowing which side of that boundary you are probing decides which range the meter goes on.

DC: steady, one direction

Direct current flows one way and holds one value. Batteries make it, and so does the output of every power supply. Circuit boards run on it: 3.3 V, 5 V, 12 V, 24 V. On the meter it is V DC, red lead positive and black negative, and a minus sign only means your probes are the other way round.

AC: reversing

Alternating current reverses direction over and over. In the United States, wall power is 120 V at 60 Hz, meaning it completes 60 full cycles each second. Much of the rest of the world uses 230 V at 50 Hz.

  • Frequency is cycles per second, in hertz. Period is the time for one cycle, and it is simply 1 divided by the frequency: 1 / 60 = about 16.7 milliseconds. At 50 Hz the period is 20 ms.
  • The 120 V on the label is an RMS value, the effective value: the steady DC voltage that would deliver the same heating power. The waveform itself swings higher, peaking near 170 V in each direction. Your meter shows the effective value; an oscilloscope shows the peaks.

Why the grid uses AC at all

Because of the transformer. Two coils wound on a shared iron core: current changing in one coil creates a changing magnetic field, and that changing field induces a voltage in the other. That is electromagnetic induction, and it is the same effect behind a generator and the back voltage a running motor produces. The ratio of turns sets the ratio of voltages. More turns on the output side steps up the voltage; fewer turns steps down. A 10-to-1 step-down transformer fed 120 V delivers 12 V, and a step-up transformer does the reverse, which is how the grid carries power at high voltage and low current.

The catch is in the word changing. A transformer only works on AC. Feed it steady DC and you get a brief pulse as you connect it and then nothing but a hot coil. That is why power is generated and distributed as AC and stepped down near the building.

An isolation transformer has equal turns, so the voltage comes out the same as it went in. Its purpose is the separation itself: there is no direct connection between the two sides, so the output does not share the building's ground reference. Hospitals use that trick in a few wet and critical areas to reduce the risk from a single fault.

Inside the power supply

A device that plugs into the wall but runs on DC has to convert, in this order:

  1. A transformer or a switching stage brings the voltage down.
  2. A rectifier, usually four diodes arranged as a bridge rectifier, flips the negative halves of the wave upward so everything flows one way. That is full-wave rectification, and the output is bumpy DC.
  3. A filter capacitor stores charge on the peaks and releases it in the dips, smoothing the bumps into something steady. What is left of the bumps is called ripple, and too much of it is a classic cause of a device behaving strangely under load.
  4. A regulator holds the output at an exact value as the load changes. A supply built with one is a regulated power supply, and its rail should read the printed value whether the device is idle or working hard.

When that whole chain lives in a block on the cord instead of inside the device, it is an AC adapter, also called an AC-to-DC adapter, or a wall transformer if it is one of the old heavy ones. Adapters wander between devices, so match the label and not the plug: the voltage, the polarity, and at least the current rating of the original, because a barrel plug that fits perfectly can still be carrying the wrong voltage.

The outlet

A standard receptacle has three contacts: the narrow slot is hot, the wider slot is neutral, and the round hole is ground. Hot carries the voltage, neutral is the normal return, and ground is the protective path that only carries current during a fault. A hospital-grade receptacle or plug is marked with a green dot: it is built to grip the blades harder and to keep its ground connection reliable, and that retention is one of the things an inspection checks.

Exam tip: three numbers. 120 V 60 Hz in the United States, about 170 V at the peak, and 16.7 ms per cycle. And one rule: transformers do nothing on DC.
Remember
DC is steady and one direction (batteries, supply rails); AC reverses, 120 V 60 Hz in the United States and 230 V 50 Hz elsewhere. Period is 1 over frequency: 16.7 ms at 60 Hz. The 120 V is the RMS or effective value and the waveform peaks near 170 V. Transformers change AC voltage by turns ratio and do nothing on DC; an isolation transformer has equal turns and just separates the sides. Inside a supply: transformer, rectifier diodes, filter capacitor, regulator. Outlet: narrow slot hot, wide slot neutral, round hole ground; hospital grade is marked with a green dot.
Deeper explanation

DC Versus AC, Transformers, and Wall Power, explained slowly

Two kinds of electricity, one boundary

Inside every mains-powered device there is a line with AC on one side and DC on the other, and that line is the power supply. Knowing which side you are probing decides the meter's range, the hazard, and what a wrong reading means.

                 DC                                AC
direction        one way, steady                   reverses, many times a second
sources          batteries, supply rails, solar    the wall outlet, generators
typical values   3.3, 5, 12, 24 V on boards        120 V at 60 Hz (United States)
                                                   230 V at 50 Hz (much of the world)
meter range      V DC                              V AC
polarity         matters: red positive             not meaningful: it alternates
transformers     do not work on it                 the reason AC is used at all

Frequency, period, and the peak

Frequency is cycles per second, measured in hertz. Period is the duration of one cycle, and it is 1 divided by the frequency.

60 Hz   ->  period = 1 / 60  = 0.0167 s = 16.7 ms
50 Hz   ->  period = 1 / 50  = 0.020 s  = 20 ms

The 120 V on the label is an RMS value: the effective value, meaning the steady DC voltage that would heat a resistor at the same rate. The waveform itself swings well past that, peaking at about 170 V in each direction (120 multiplied by about 1.414). Your multimeter reports the effective value, which is the useful number; an oscilloscope draws the peaks, which is why the two instruments appear to disagree about the same outlet.

And 60 Hz is not a neutral detail. Reversing 60 times a second lands near the worst case for disturbing the heart's own electrical timing, and it is also why 60 Hz hum is the background noise every biomedical amplifier is designed to reject.

Transformers

Two coils sharing an iron core. A changing current in the first coil creates a changing magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field induces a voltage in the second. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio.

Turns ratio (primary : secondary)   Fed 120 V   Result
10 : 1                              120 V       12 V, stepped down
1 : 2                               120 V       240 V, stepped up
1 : 1                               120 V       120 V, isolated only

Power in roughly equals power out, so a step-down transformer delivers lower voltage at higher current. And the whole mechanism depends on change, which is why a transformer does nothing on steady DC except get hot: connect DC and you see one brief pulse, then nothing.

An isolation transformer is a 1:1 transformer whose purpose is the gap itself. There is no conductive path between input and output, so the output does not reference the building's ground, and a single fault from either output conductor to ground does not complete a circuit through a person. Hospitals use isolated power in a few wet and critical locations, monitored by a line isolation monitor that warns when the isolation has degraded.

What is inside a linear power supply

mains AC -> transformer (step down) -> rectifier diodes (one direction only)
         -> filter capacitor (smooth the bumps) -> regulator (hold it exact) -> DC out

Each stage has a signature failure. An open rectifier diode turns full-wave into half-wave rectification: the ripple drops to 60 Hz, which you hear as a hum, and the supply sags under load. A dried-out filter capacitor leaves ripple on the rail, and ripple shows up as noise on a trace, erratic readings, or random resets under load. A failed regulator gives a rail that is too high, too low, or that collapses the moment the device does any work.

The outlet

Three contacts: the narrow slot is hot, the wide slot is neutral, the round hole is ground. Hot carries the supply, neutral is the working return, and ground carries nothing at all until something has gone wrong. A hospital-grade receptacle or plug is marked with a green dot, built for blade retention and a reliable ground path, and receptacle testing checks exactly those two things plus correct polarity.
